seo.best_title: The First Job Is Older Than Humans
seo.description_hook: What was the first job in history? The oldest stone tools are 3.3 million years old, older than humans themselves, and the first famous name in history belonged to an accountant.
paragraphs: In this animated history of work we start with the Lomekwi stone tools in Kenya, look at roles in hunter-gatherer groups, the grandmother hypothesis, and the 9,000 year old female hunter from the Andes.

Then we visit 45,000 year old cave art in Sulawesi, the cared-for Neanderthal of Shanidar Cave, the Standard Professions List from Uruk, Kushim the first named person, workers paid in bread and beer, and the famous complaint against Ea-nasir.
We finish in Egypt with pyramid work gangs like the Drunkards of Menkaure, and the first recorded strike at Deir el-Medina.
sources: Harmand et al. - 3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya, Nature (2015)
Hawkes et al. - Grandmothering, menopause, and the evolution of human life histories, PNAS (1998)
Haas et al. - Female hunters of the early Americas, Science Advances (2020)
Brumm et al. - Oldest cave art found in Sulawesi, Science Advances (2021)
Englund & Nissen - Die lexikalischen Listen der archaischen Texte aus Uruk (1993)
A. Leo Oppenheim - Letters from Mesopotamia (1967), letter of Nanni to Ea-nasir
Mark Lehner & Zahi Hawass - Giza and the Pyramids (2017)
William F. Edgerton - The Strikes in Ramses III's Twenty-Ninth Year, JNES (1951)

shots.say: Right now, millions of people are sitting at work, counting the minutes.
Some are in offices. Some are in kitchens. Some are pretending to be busy.
Maybe that's you right now. No judgment.
But have you ever wondered who had the very first job?

shots.title: OLDER THAN...
shots.say: Because work is older than writing. Older than money. Older than farming.
And the first job might be older than humans.

shots.title: TODAY
shots.say: Today: a three million year old job, the first boss, beer salaries, and the first strike.
Clock in. Let's go.

shots.label: KENYA
shots.say: Our story starts in Kenya, near Lake Turkana.
About three point three million years ago.
Someone sat down and smashed one rock against another.
shots.ai: an early ape-like human sitting in dry grassland knapping stones

shots.say: They made sharp stone flakes. The oldest stone tools ever found.
The site is called Lomekwi 3. The tools were described in 2015.
shots.label: LOMEKWI 3

shots.say: Here's the thing. That's older than our whole genus.
But here's the weird part.
No one is sure which species made them.
Maybe an early ape-like relative. Not a human at all.
shots.ai: a cartoon early hominin ape holding a sharp stone tool

shots.say: So the first job in history might be: toolmaker. And the worker wasn't even human.

shots.say: Fast forward to real humans. Hunter-gatherers.
Did they have jobs? Not with job titles. But they had roles.

shots.title: STONE AGE ROLES
shots.say: Hunting, gathering, making tools, keeping the fire going.
And the most important job of all? Looking after kids.
Some scientists think grandmothers were the secret weapon.
Grandmothers gathered food and helped raise kids, so mothers could have more children.
It's called the grandmother hypothesis. And yes, it's a real theory.
Like every big idea in human evolution, people still argue about it.

shots.say: Now, you've probably heard: men hunted, women gathered.

shots.label: ANDES
shots.say: In 2018, archaeologists in Peru dug up a 9,000 year old burial.
The person was buried with a full hunting kit. Stone points and tools.
shots.label: HUNTING KIT
shots.ai: a stone age burial with spear points and tools laid out in the Andes

shots.say: Everyone assumed it was a man. Then they checked.
It was a woman. A big game hunter.
Thousands of years of assumptions. Gone in one test.
How common were female hunters? Historians still disagree.
But clearly, the job board was less strict than we thought.

shots.say: Some jobs were about more than food.

shots.label: SULAWESI
shots.say: On the island of Sulawesi, in Indonesia, there's a cave painting.
It shows a wild pig. And it's at least forty-five thousand years old.
shots.label: CAVE PIG
shots.ai: an ancient red ochre cave painting of a wild pig on a cave wall

shots.say: Someone spent hours painting a pig. Art might be one of our oldest jobs.
And then there's healing.

shots.label: SHANIDAR CAVE
shots.say: In Shanidar Cave in Iraq, archaeologists found a Neanderthal man.
He had a crushed arm, a damaged eye, and probably couldn't hear well.
But he lived for years. Someone must have looked after him.
Caring for the sick may be one of humanity's oldest jobs too.

shots.say: Then, about twelve thousand years ago, came farming.
Farming produced something new. Extra food.
shots.ai: an early farmer working a wheat field with a cow nearby

shots.say: And extra food meant not everyone had to find food anymore.

shots.title: SURPLUS = JOBS
shots.say: Extra food, bigger villages, and suddenly, brand new jobs.

shots.title: NEW JOBS
shots.say: Potters, brewers, builders, guards, and of course, chiefs.
Farming gave us bread, beer, and bosses.
Two out of three isn't bad.

shots.say: But jobs with real titles? For that, we need writing.

shots.label: URUK
shots.say: And writing starts in Mesopotamia, in a city called Uruk.
Around five thousand two hundred years ago.
Scribes wrote a list of job titles on clay. Over a hundred of them.
shots.label: JOB LIST

shots.say: Historians call it the Standard Professions List.
Scribes copied it for centuries, like homework.

shots.title: ON THE LIST
shots.say: Leaders, officials, priests, cooks, fishermen, potters.
And what job is at the very top of the list?
Some kind of top leader. Probably the boss.
Five thousand years later, the boss is still at the top of the list.

shots.say: Here's something even stranger.
One of the oldest names in all of history appears on a clay tablet from Uruk.
shots.label: KUSHIM

shots.say: The name is Kushim.
Was Kushim a king? A hero? A great warrior?
No. Kushim was probably an accountant.

shots.title: KUSHIM'S TABLET
shots.say: The tablet records barley stored over thirty-seven months, signed by Kushim.
The first famous person in history did paperwork.
To be fair, some experts think Kushim was a job title, not a name.
Either way, the first written records are about work. And grain.

shots.say: So how did people get paid? No coins existed yet.

shots.title: SUMER PAYCHECK
shots.say: Workers were paid in rations. Barley, bread, and beer.
Archaeologists find thousands of cheap, identical clay bowls in these cities.
shots.label: RATION BOWLS

shots.say: Many think they were ration bowls. One bowl, one day's grain.
So your salary was, literally, a bowl.
And on good days, a jug of beer.

shots.say: And where there are jobs, there are angry customers.

shots.label: UR
shots.say: Around 1750 BC, in the city of Ur, a man named Nanni wrote a letter.
He'd paid a merchant called Ea-nasir for copper. The copper was bad.
shots.ai: an angry Mesopotamian customer confronting a nervous merchant over copper

shots.say: It's often called the oldest customer complaint in history.
Nanni says he was treated with contempt. He wants a refund. Now.
Today, that tablet sits in the British Museum.
Ea-nasir is now famous online. For the worst reason possible.

shots.label: GIZA
shots.say: Now, Egypt. The pyramid builders.
They weren't slaves, as people often think. Most were organized, paid workers.
shots.ai: teams of stick figure workers dragging stone blocks toward a pyramid

shots.say: They worked in teams. And the teams had names.

shots.title: REAL GANG NAMES
shots.say: Archaeologists found names like Friends of Khufu, and Drunkards of Menkaure.
Drunkards of Menkaure. That's a real team name. Carved in stone.
Every office has that one team.

shots.say: Around eleven fifty-seven B C, near the Valley of the Kings.
The village of Deir el-Medina housed the skilled workers who built royal tombs.
shots.label: DEIR EL-MEDINA
shots.ai: an ancient Egyptian workers village of mud brick houses near desert cliffs

shots.say: They were paid in grain. And the grain was late. Again.
So the workers did something nobody had recorded before.
They put down their tools and walked out.
It's the first recorded strike in history.
A scribe wrote it all down on papyrus. It still exists.
And it worked. Eventually, the rations came.

shots.title: THE HISTORY OF WORK
shots.say: Toolmakers, artists, accountants, angry customers, and strikers.
So what was the first job in history?
If you mean any work at all, it's probably making tools.
If you mean the first job title written down, it was the boss.
And the first famous worker was an accountant. Sorry, accountants.
But one question is still open.
How did people pay for things before money was invented?
